This isn't a scene from a film. This is a heartbreaking reality that still exists in parts of Nepal. For some women and girls, getting their period means being sent away from their own home to spend the night in a small shed, away from their families. They are left to face cold nights, fear, loneliness, and the danger of snakes, insects, and wild animals—all because of a natural biological process. Menstruation should never be a reason for exclusion or shame. Take a moment and ask yourself: If it were someone you love—your daughter, your sister, your wife, or your mother—would you accept this as "tradition"? Some customs deserve to be questioned, especially when they put lives and dignity at risk. Every woman deserves to feel safe, respected, and valued, no matter what day of the month it is. Let's raise awareness, start conversations, and stand together to end harmful practices like this. Something Was Found in Flooded Nepal That Could Not Have Been There When the floods swept through Nepal, the water did not just cause damage, it dragged impossible things into the light. Ambrose Wild walks you through ten of them, from a sea fossil stranded high in the mountains and a boulder no ordinary river should be able to move, to cliff tombs no living person can climb and a capital built on the floor of a vanished lake. For each one you get the real, measurable explanation instead of a mystery, including how ocean floors were lifted into the sky and how highlanders inherited a survival gene from a lost human species. By the end, you see why none of it is a miracle, just the strange scale of the Himalaya. #Nepal #Himalaya #Geology #Archaeology #AncientMysteries

Nepali police have honoured their canine colleagues as part of Tihar for their contributions to criminal investigations, security operations and search and rescue missions, including their efforts in Rasuwa flood recovery missions. In Nepal, the second day of Tihar, called Kukur Puja, is dedicated to dogs. Armed Police Force officer Ramesh Pokhrel said dogs were regarded as the “messengers of Yamaraj, the god of death, as well as manifestations of God”. “This is their special day, and we worship them to make them happy and show our love and respect for them,” Pokhrel said. During the ceremonies, dogs were lined up and adorned with flower garlands and vermilion tika (a red mark on the forehead), and some were awarded medals. Read more stories @sbsnews_au (link in bio).
